transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-26 11:00 PT / 14:00 ET, duration ~42m. Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Miguel (Orchid Head of ML), Priya (Platform Engineer), Karen (CTO).

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro, I'm Samira Patel, AE at Redwood, and with me is Daniel Cho our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Miguel: Hi, thanks, Miguel here. Excited to see the model catalog, we skimmed the docs.
[00:12] Daniel: Awesome, we'll do a quick product walkthrough — console, API, then Optimize — and focus on picking open models for your use case and what the benchmarks mean.
[00:22] Priya: Sounds good, first question: we handle PHI, so VPC/private deployment options are mandatory, SOC2 is required, and we need KMS integration.
[00:30] Samira: Totally, we have Private deployments with customer-managed networking and KMS/HSM integrations — we'll attach the SOC2 packet after.
[00:38] Karen: Great. Miguel, quickly: what are your latency targets?
[00:41] Miguel: For short prompts (<=128 tokens) we want p50 <150ms, p95 ideally <400ms. Also budget constraints — want to compare cost vs latency.
[00:51] Daniel: That's helpful. Ok jumping into the console — I'm sharing screen. You'll see the model catalog page; we surface open models with verified benchmark badges, like popper... uh, Pythia family, Llama variants, Mistral — and we include performance profiles per sequence length and hardware.
[01:12] Daniel: Note: some names in the transcript might be mis-typed, the console shows detailed compatibility. Here is the compatibility matrix row: model -> quantization support -> recommended GPU -> tokenizer differences -> KV cache compatibility.
[01:28] Miguel: Can you show an example where a model is good for low-latency short prompts?
[01:33] Daniel: Sure, see 'redwood-llama-70b-quant' tag — for short sequences it hits low latency on A10/RTX6000 class GPUs with 8-bit quant. But for strict p50 <150ms you'll likely pick a smaller family like Mistral-instruct-7B or a trimmed Pythia. We also show tokens/sec numbers for batched vs single requests.
[01:56] Priya: How reliable are these numbers? Are they from your hosted infra or synthetic runs?
[02:02] Daniel: Good question — benchmarks in the catalog come from our verification harness running on representative hardware; each badge links to the raw CSV and run configuration. We also do cross-variant runs to show performance post-quantization. We'll share the raw CSV.
[02:16] Miguel: We typically have bursty traffic driven by chat sessions and scheduled batch jobs overnight. How does batching affect latency?
[02:23] Daniel: Batching improves throughput but increases tail latency for single requests. Our Optimize tool will recommend batching window sizes based on your latency SLOs and traffic patterns; for chat you might use smaller batch sizes and prefix caching to keep p50 low.
[02:36] Karen: What about tokenizer mismatches? We use a custom tokenizer pipeline in production.
[02:41] Daniel: The compatibility matrix flags tokenization differences and suggests mapping strategies. If you have a custom tokenizer we can run a tokenization delta check — that can be part of the pilot.
[02:52] Samira: Back to cost vs latency: we show estimated unit cost per 1k tokens at different configurations (batch size, quant level, GPU family). For instance, a 7B 8-bit quant model can be 3-4x cheaper than a 70B float model with comparable instr quality for many tasks.
[03:08] Miguel: How do you handle fallback when a model isn't available in a region or capacity tier?
[03:13] Daniel: Smart routing: requests route by region/tier and fallback to compatible variants automatically. You can pin model versions and set policies.
[03:20] Priya: For Private deployment, does the compatibility matrix change? e.g., some quant libs depend on specific drivers.
[03:26] Daniel: Yes, the matrix includes per-deployment notes; certain quant profiles require newer CUDA/cuDNN or specific runtimes. We include kernel and lib versions per entry.
[03:35] Miguel: Could you walk through an example benchmark CSV?
[03:39] Daniel: Sure — here's a sample: columns are model, hardware, batch_size, seq_len, p50, p95, tokens_per_sec, memory_gb, quant_flags. You'll see rows for single-request latency and for batched throughput. We also flag where an AVX mismatch or tokenizer difference caused anomalies — transcription sometimes shows those as k8s issues but it's actually runtime kernel mismatch.
[04:05] Miguel: I saw a note about KV cache compatibility — is that about stateful chat?
[04:09] Daniel: Exactly — models that support persistent KV cache let you keep context without re-encoding tokens each turn. The matrix shows whether KV cache is supported in each quantization path and if it's efficient for large context.
[04:21] Priya: For our HIPAA scope, audit logs are non-negotiable. How granular are the logs?
[04:26] Samira: Console-level tracing provides per-request token counts, latency, route, and model version; Private gives you full audit logs and optional retention controls. We'll attach sample log schema.
[04:36] Karen: On the API side, is streaming supported and does it affect cost or latency metrics?
[04:41] Daniel: Streaming is supported; it changes perceived latency because you can start returning tokens earlier. Our benchmarks include both non-stream and streaming token throughput metrics. Cost is based on tokens emitted, so streaming doesn't change unit cost but can improve user experience.
[04:56] Miguel: Are there any gotchas around safety filters or model behavior differences across variants?
[05:01] Daniel: Yes, smaller models or aggressive quantization can shift behavior. The catalog ties quality metrics — like eval scores on our customer prompts — to each model entry. We recommend running a short eval set during pilot to detect regressions.
[05:15] Samira: We'll include Redwood Optimize recommendations in the pilot: which models to try, recommended quant levels, and batching/caching config tuned for your load.
[05:24] Priya: For the pilot, we'd want to run three candidate models: a smaller 7B, a mid 13-15B, and a bigger 33-70B to compare cost/accuracy/latency. Is that feasible?
[05:33] Daniel: Totally. We often do side-by-side pilot runs. We'll provide the compatibility matrix so you can see which quant profiles and hardware map to those families.
[05:42] Miguel: What about tokenizer offsets when comparing outputs across models? We need deterministic behavior for A/B testing.
[05:48] Daniel: We can normalize tokenization and provide token-level diffs. For determinism we recommend fixing seeds and using our SDK's deterministic sampling (or greedy) config during evaluation.
[05:59] Priya: Any notes about integration complexity for our infra? We're on AWS, EKS, and use Vault for secrets.
[06:05] Daniel: For Private on AWS we support VPC peering and private endpoints; for secrets you can use KMS or HashiCorp Vault via our integrations. The deployment package includes Helm charts for EKS. Some customers run the control plane in their VPC and the runtime on-prem.
[06:20] Miguel: Pricing — do you have a ballpark for reserved dedicated capacity vs hosted?
[06:24] Samira: We'll send a tiered pricing deck, but generally dedicated reserved capacity is more predictable and cheaper per-unit at scale, hosted is easier to start with. We have burst capacity and autoscaling policies.
[06:37] Karen: For compliance, can we get the SOC2 + ISO docs and a vendor questionnaire?
[06:41] Samira: Yes, I'll send SOC2 + security pack and a redwood vendor questionnaire template.
[06:46] Daniel: Back to the console: you can filter the catalog by quality badges, latency buckets, hardware compatibility, and tags like "medical-vetted". We also surface model lineage and commit hashes for reproducibility.
[06:59] Miguel: How do you handle model updates / rollouts? We want canary deploys and automatic fallback if quality regresses.
[07:05] Daniel: We support rollout policies (canary, A/B) and automatic fallback to previous model versions; trace-based quality alerts tie to prompt sets so you can detect regressions.
[07:16] Priya: One practical question: tokenization library versions — how strict are they? If we upgrade tokenizer in our pipeline, will the model outputs differ?
[07:23] Daniel: Yes, changes in tokenizer version can change tokenization boundaries; the compatibility matrix tracks tested tokenizer versions. We'll do a tokenization delta check as part of pilot.
[07:34] Miguel: Ok let's talk evaluation: what's the recommended eval set size to be meaningful?
[07:38] Daniel: For conversational flows 500-1k prompts is a good start. For high-stakes outputs you may want 2-3k. We can run evals in our sandbox and provide per-model eval reports.
[07:50] Samira: Quick recap: we'll share pricing deck, SOC2/security docs, benchmark CSVs, compatibility matrix, and run pilot evals on three models. Daniel will lead the benchmark runs.
[08:05] Karen: That works. Miguel, any timelines?
[08:08] Miguel: We'd like to start pilot in early April, target running benchmarks week of April 6.
[08:13] Priya: I'll send infra diagram and VPC reqs by Monday.
[08:17] Daniel: Perfect. Any more questions on model selection?
[08:20] Miguel: One last — do you support custom fine-tuned variants of open models in the catalog?
[08:24] Daniel: Yes, you can bring tuned weights; we support hosting fine-tuned variants and list compatibility notes. For Private, you can keep weights in your registry and we pull them into runtime during deployment.
[08:36] Miguel: Good. Thanks a lot.
[08:39] Samira: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and set a pilot kickoff.

[08:45] End of recorded transcript (the timestamps after ~8m are shorthand; actual call continued ~42 minutes with Q&A and sidebars).

Notes on transcription quality: occasional misrecognitions of model names (e.g., "Pythia" transcribed as "Pita"), and some speaker labels merged. Raw benchmark links referenced: [benchmark-csv link], [compatibility-matrix link], [security-pack link].

Meeting closed: 11:42 PT.
